lead: A factor of safety is the number that turns a measured strength into the stress a designer allows. It covers loads that are only estimated, strengths that scatter from batch to batch, simplified stress formulas and the cost of a failure. Design codes and standards are the published rulebooks that fix minimum factors, methods and materials, so that two engineers sizing the same part reach the same defensible answer. Before either is chosen, the designer must know how the part can fail.
prereq: You need the properties from material selection.

blocks.text: A part has failed when it can no longer do its job safely, which can happen long before it breaks.

items: Yielding: a ductile part deforms permanently when stress reaches Syt; a bent lever is a failure.
Fracture: a brittle part (cast iron) breaks suddenly near Sut without warning.
Excessive deflection: a shaft or frame bends or twists enough to misalign gears or spoil accuracy, while still strong.
Fatigue: a crack grows under repeated stress far below Sut; see failure theories and fatigue design.
Buckling, wear, corrosion and creep: a slender strut collapses sideways; surfaces wear away; rust thins a section; a hot part stretches slowly with time.

blocks.text: The mode fixes which strength goes on top of the factor of safety.

sections.h3: Factor of safety and allowable stress

blocks.text: n = failure stress/allowable stress; σallow = Syt/n (ductile) or Sut/n (brittle)

n is the factor of safety (no unit, n > 1); S<sub>yt</sub> and S<sub>ut</sub> are the yield and ultimate tensile strengths (MPa); σ<sub>allow</sub> is the allowable or permissible stress (MPa). The part is safe when the working stress σ ≤ σ<sub>allow</sub>, that is, when the actual factor of safety S/σ is at least the required n.

items: Choose the strength for the failure mode: S<sub>yt</sub> for a ductile part, S<sub>ut</sub> for a brittle one.
Choose the required n from a code or from judgement (below).
Find the working stress from the load and section (see direct, bending and torsional stresses).
Compare; if σ > σ<sub>allow</sub>, enlarge the section or change the material.

blocks.text: The factor grows with uncertainty. Typical textbook values: steady load on ductile steel, 1.5 to 2 on yield; brittle materials, 3 to 4 on ultimate (the strength scatters and failure gives no warning); shock loads, 3 or more; lifting equipment and pressure vessels, fixed by their codes. A larger n is not free: it means a heavier and costlier part. The margin of safety is n − 1, so n = 2.5 is a margin of 1.5.

A standard fixes agreed sizes, materials, tests and dimensions so that parts from different makers fit and behave alike; a code is a standard that sets design rules for safety: load cases, stress methods, minimum factors, tests and marking. A code is followed because law, a contract or an inspector requires it. Examples: the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code; ISO 286 for limits and fits and ISO 3 for preferred numbers; and the Indian Standards of the Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS), such as IS 1570 for the designation of steels, IS 919 for limits and fits and IS 2062 for structural steel. Some syllabi call this exposure to standards.

Codes may replace one factor of safety with partial factors: the nominal resistance R is reduced by a resistance factor φ ≤ 1 and each load effect Q is raised by a load factor γ ≥ 1, and the check becomes φR ≥ ΣγQ. Loads and strengths scatter differently (a dead weight is better known than wind), so splitting the margin keeps the reliability even. Codes are the minimum, they lag new materials, and they cover only the failure modes they list: a code-compliant part can still fail by fatigue, corrosion or misuse.

examples.question: A ductile steel tie of cross-section 250 mm² carries a steady pull of 45 kN. S<sub>yt</sub> = 280 MPa and the required factor of safety is 2.5 on yield. Find the allowable stress and the working stress, decide whether the tie is safe, and find the smallest standard round bar (20, 22, 25 mm) that is.
steps: Units: 1 MPa = 1 N/mm²; F = 45 kN = 45,000 N.
Since 180 > 112 the tie is not safe; its actual factor of safety is 280/180 = 1.56, below 2.5.
Area needed: A = F/σ<sub>allow</sub> = 45,000/112 = 401.8 mm², so d = √(4A/π) = √(4 × 401.8/π) = 22.6 mm.
Bars: 20 mm gives 314.2 mm² and 22 mm gives 380.1 mm², both too small; 25 mm gives 490.9 mm², stress 45,000/490.9 = 91.7 MPa, actual n = 280/91.7 = 3.05.
examples.answer: σ<sub>allow</sub> = 112 MPa, working stress 180 MPa, so the 250 mm² tie is unsafe; at least 402 mm² is needed, and a 25 mm bar (91.7 MPa, n = 3.05) is the smallest that passes.

examples.question: A link of grey cast iron FG 200 (S<sub>ut</sub> = 200 MPa) carries a steady pull of 12 kN. The code asks for a factor of safety of 4 on ultimate. Find the side of a square section, rounded up to a whole millimetre, and the actual factor of safety.
steps: Cast iron is brittle, so use S<sub>ut</sub>: σ<sub>allow</sub> = 200/4 = 50 MPa.
Area needed: A = 12,000/50 = 240 mm². Side a = √240 = 15.5 mm, rounded up to 16 mm.
Actual factor of safety = 200/46.9 = 4.27, above the required 4.
examples.answer: A 16 mm × 16 mm section: stress 46.9 MPa, actual factor of safety 4.27.

traps: Using S<sub>ut</sub> for a ductile part that fails by yielding. A mild steel tie that stretches at 280 MPa is not saved by an S<sub>ut</sub> of 450 MPa.
Mixing kN and MPa: 45 kN on 250 mm² is 45,000/250 = 180 MPa, not 0.18 MPa.
Confusing the factor of safety with the margin: n = 2.5 is a margin of 1.5 (150 %).
Treating a code as a factor of safety. A code is a document; it may fix n, or replace it by partial factors.
Assuming a large n makes any design safe. If the wrong failure mode was checked (yield instead of deflection or fatigue), the factor protects nothing.

quiz.q: Define factor of safety for a ductile and for a brittle material.
quiz.a: Ductile: n = S<sub>yt</sub>/σ<sub>allow</sub>. Brittle: n = S<sub>ut</sub>/σ<sub>allow</sub>. It has no unit and is greater than 1.

quiz.q: List four modes of failure of machine parts.
quiz.a: Yielding, fracture, excessive deflection, fatigue (also buckling, wear, corrosion, creep).

quiz.q: Why is a larger factor of safety used for a cast-iron bracket than for a rolled-steel tie under the same steady load?
quiz.a: Cast iron is brittle: it breaks without yielding, so there is no warning and no redistribution of stress, and its strength scatters more because of casting defects. Rolled steel yields first and has repeatable properties.

quiz.q: Distinguish a standard from a design code.
quiz.a: A standard fixes sizes, materials and tests so parts are interchangeable (ISO 286, IS 1570). A code sets design rules for safety, with load cases, methods and minimum factors, and is enforced by law or contract (the ASME pressure vessel code).

quiz.q: A brittle part has S<sub>ut</sub> = 420 MPa and the code asks for n = 4. Find the allowable stress.
A tie of 300 mm² carries 60 kN; S<sub>yt</sub> = 250 MPa and n = 2.5. Check it.
quiz.a: Working stress 60,000/300 = 200 MPa; allowable 250/2.5 = 100 MPa. Unsafe: actual n = 250/200 = 1.25.

quiz.q: A designer uses n = 2 on S<sub>ut</sub> = 410 MPa for a mild steel lever with S<sub>yt</sub> = 250 MPa. What is wrong, and what factor on yield does the lever really have?
quiz.a: The allowable is 410/2 = 205 MPa, so the true factor against yielding is only 250/205 = 1.22, not 2. Yielding governs a ductile lever, so S<sub>yt</sub> must be used.

quiz.q: Why do limit-state codes use a load factor above 1 and a resistance factor below 1 instead of one factor of safety?
quiz.a: Loads and strengths have different scatter. Separate factors can be calibrated against data for each, so a well-known dead load gets a small factor and wind or live load a larger one, and reliability stays similar across materials.

beyond: Reliability-based design treats loads and strengths as random variables and states safety as a probability of failure or a reliability index β instead of a single factor. Codes calibrate their partial factors this way, and ISO 2394 gives the general principles. Search next for reliability index, partial safety factors and stress-strength interference.
